item.title: Behavioural interventions shift carbon-pricing support only slightly
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02628-9

Across 55 independently designed experiments with 19,558 participants from the USA, behavioural interventions produced a small increase in support for carbon pricing. Participating researchers substantially overestimated these effects.
item.dc:title: Behavioural interventions shift carbon-pricing support only slightly

item.title: Neural interface without a scalpel
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02572-8

For people who are paralysed by spinal cord injury, regaining hand use is a top priority. Yet the most capable neural interfaces have relied on surgically implanted electrodes. Yang, Rawji, Gibbs and colleagues show that individual motor units, read non-invasively using surface electrodes, can deliver multidimensional control even amid involuntary background muscle activity.
item.dc:title: Neural interface without a scalpel
item.dc:creator: Michael Dimitriou

item.title: Research that will survive a fast-paced world
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02643-w

Crises and technological waves pull science towards fast, trend-driven work. But a drift towards timely research might negatively affect quality and limit the methods, infrastructure and datasets that accumulate value slowly. We discuss how researchers, funders and journals can draw lasting value from urgency-driven research.
item.dc:title: Research that will survive a fast-paced world
item.dc:creator: Edmond Awad
Katarzyna Doniec
Gerd Gigerenzer

item.title: Multidimensional motor unit control after paralysing spinal cord injury using non-invasive recordings
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02626-x

Yang, Rawji, Gibbs and colleagues show that participants with spinal cord injury can modulate the activity of motor units from their paralysed hand to control a computer cursor in 3D, play video games and drive a virtual wheelchair.
item.dc:title: Multidimensional motor unit control after paralysing spinal cord injury using non-invasive recordings

item.title: Fifty-five crowdsourced designs assessing carbon pricing support in the USA
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02629-8

In 55 experiments involving nearly 20,000 US residents, behavioural efforts to build public support for carbon pricing raised support by only 1.1–2.4 percentage points.
item.dc:title: Fifty-five crowdsourced designs assessing carbon pricing support in the USA

item.title: Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02615-0

This Review evaluates evidence for eight pressing concerns about how AI is affecting people. It finds modest support for the most alarming claims but calls for deeper scrutiny of the human impact of AI.
item.dc:title: Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
